    Cell and cell-type level scores and p-values

    HeterogeneityTest.Rmd

    SCADS produces two kinds of inference. At the level of a single cell, a disease relevance score with a p-value. At the level of a cell type, a test of whether the cells within it differ from one another in disease relevance. This vignette gives both formulas and shows how to run them.

    The cell score

    Each cell’s score is the enrichment of disease heritability in its open regions relative to genome-wide, reconstructed from the topic model:

    ci=∑k∑jlikIkjekvj∑k∑jlikIkjvj=∑kwikek,∑kwik=1c_i = \frac{\sum_k\sum_j l_{ik} I_{kj} e_k v_j}{\sum_k\sum_j l_{ik} I_{kj} v_j} = \sum_k w_{ik}\, e_k, \qquad \sum_k w_{ik} = 1

    where likl_{ik} is the cell’s loading on topic kk, IkjI_{kj} marks region jj as open in topic kk, and eke_k is that topic’s heritability enrichment from S-LDSC. The weights wik∝likskw_{ik} \propto l_{ik} s_k depend on the loadings and the topic annotation sizes sks_k, and sum to one, so ci=1c_i = 1 when no topic is enriched.

    The score is a linear function of the enrichment estimates, so its variance is a quadratic form in their covariance Σ\Sigma:

    Var(ĉi)=∑k∑mwikwimΣkm\mathrm{Var}(\hat c_i) = \sum_k \sum_m w_{ik}\, w_{im}\, \Sigma_{km}

    summed over all ordered pairs. The p-value tests ci=1c_i = 1:

    zi=ĉi−1Var(ĉi)z_i = \frac{\hat c_i - 1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\hat c_i)}}

    The cell-type heterogeneity test

    For a cell type gg, let SgS_g be the covariance of the weight vectors ww across its cells. The within-type variance of the score is

    Tg=Varg(c)=Ê′SgÊT_g = \mathrm{Var}_g(c) = \hat E' S_g \hat E

    The null is that all topics are equally enriched, E=c𝟏E = c\mathbf{1} for an unknown cc — not that nothing is enriched. If every topic shares the same enrichment then every cell scores cc and the within-type variance is zero regardless of the loadings.

    Because the weights sum to one, Sg𝟏=0S_g\mathbf{1} = 0 exactly, so writing Ê=c𝟏+ε\hat E = c\mathbf{1} + \varepsilon with ε∼N(0,Σ)\varepsilon \sim N(0,\Sigma) removes every term in cc:

    Tg=ε′Sgε∼∑jλjχ12,λ=eig(Σ1/2SgΣ1/2)T_g = \varepsilon' S_g \varepsilon \sim \sum_j \lambda_j \chi^2_1, \qquad \lambda = \mathrm{eig}\!\left(\Sigma^{1/2} S_g \Sigma^{1/2}\right)

    The p-value is exact by Imhof inversion. No permutation is involved, and the unknown level cc never has to be estimated.

    Cell scores and p-values

    scads() computes these as part of the pipeline:

    res <- scads(...)          # see vignette("StepByStep")

res$cs_res$cs         # per-cell score
res$cs_res$p_cell     # per-cell p-value, one per cell
res$cs_res$var_cell   # per-cell variance
res$cs_res$Sigma_used # covariance of the topic enrichments

fdr <- p.adjust(res$cs_res$p_cell, "BH")

    p_cell is NA where the variance is zero, so it always aligns with cs. alternative = "greater" gives a one-sided test of enrichment; the default is two-sided, which also flags significantly depleted cells.

    Cell-type heterogeneity 

    ht <- cell_type_heterogeneity(
  topic_res  = res$out1,
  enrichment = res$cs_res$ldsc_res_table$Enrichment,
  Sigma      = res$cs_res$Sigma_used,
  groups     = cell_type_labels   # one label per cell, in Lmat row order
)

subset(ht, fdr < 0.05)

    groups can be published cell-type labels, clusters, or any partition of the cells. Groups smaller than min_cells (default 20) are skipped and NA labels dropped. The result gives cell_type, n, the statistic, p and BH-adjusted fdr, sorted by p-value.

    Interpreting the results

    Score spread does not predict heterogeneity. TgT_g and its null eigenvalues both scale linearly with SgS_g, so the p-value is invariant to the overall size of within-group variation. What matters is whether the direction in which cells vary aligns with the direction in which topic enrichments differ. A cell type with a wide score range can be non-significant, and a narrow one significant.

    Test association before heterogeneity. Heterogeneity within a cell type that carries no overall disease signal is heterogeneity in noise.

    Power follows the precision of the topic enrichments, not the number of cells. The test sees only differences between topics, so a trait with large but imprecisely estimated enrichments can give no detections while a trait with a smaller, tighter spread detects readily.

    Loadings are treated as fixed. Topic-model uncertainty is not propagated into either variance.

    Following up a significant cell type

    The test says that cells within a cell type differ; it does not say which cells, or along what axis. Correlating the cell score against the topic loadings within that cell type identifies the topics driving the gradient, and their annotations point at the regulatory programs responsible.
